questions.prompt: A TWAP schedule must buy 9,000 shares from 10:00 to 16:00 in slices every 30 minutes. How many shares does each child order buy?
questions.explanation: Six hours hold 12 slices of 30 minutes. Equal slices give 9,000 / 12 = 750 shares each.

questions.prompt: Splitting 2,000 shares into 4 orders of 500 cut the average cost from $0.0265 to $0.014 above the mid price. Which assumption does that saving depend on?
options: That the commission is lower on small orders
That the bid-ask spread is zero
That every child order fills at the mid price
That the book refills to the same shape before each slice
questions.explanation: Each 500-share slice paid $100.024 only because 300 shares waited again at $100.02 and 200 at $100.03. If the book does not refill, or the price rises between slices, the saving shrinks or disappears.

questions.prompt: Why do real schedules move each child order's start time by a random number of seconds?
options: So other traders find it harder to spot the regular pattern and buy ahead of it
So the total number of shares bought changes from day to day
So each child order pays a smaller commission
So the parent order finishes before the window ends
questions.explanation: An order that arrives every 30 minutes on the dot is easy to notice. Other traders who notice it can buy first and sell to you at a higher price.
